entry.title: feat(anki): read Anki again when the learner comes back from it
entry.content:
feat(anki): read Anki again when the learner comes back from it

The cooldown protects a bridge from an app that regains focus repeatedly, but
the learner who answered three cards and came straight back is the case it got
wrong: those answers are why they returned. A genuine hidden-to-visible
transition now reads once past it, the focus event that follows joins that read,
and a read already running when they returned gets exactly one follow-up queued
behind it rather than one per event.

Every successful commit publishes its revision, whether or not the word list
changed. An evening of study leaves the same words proving something different,
and a word count is the one thing that cannot notice that.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(vocabulary): keep the practice words a story asks for stable whi…
entry.content:
feat(vocabulary): keep the practice words a story asks for stable while chosen

The preview holds one immutable capture and redraws only when something asks:
a new capture, a changed setting, an edited choice, or Shuffle. Reading the list
never redraws it, so it cannot change under a learner mid-decision, and Generate
receives the list that was on screen rather than a fresh sample.

Manual picks survive shuffles and refreshes by expression; one the vocabulary no
longer has is reported rather than sent, and one that no longer fits a shortened
story is named instead of dropped. A removal takes its slot with it. A failed
read keeps the words already shown and says it kept them.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(persistence): read the vocabulary at one revision and refuse to …
entry.content:
feat(persistence): read the vocabulary at one revision and refuse to clobber it

The snapshot id stays stable so a generated story keeps one link to the current
vocabulary, which means it cannot say whether the words behind it changed. Every
commit now writes a revision that can, including one that changed only what a
source proved about recent study.

A capture reads the snapshot, its expressions and its sources in one read
transaction, so a refresh landing mid-read cannot produce a selection whose
words, evidence and provenance come from different vocabularies. A build that
names the revision it was prepared against is refused rather than written over a
newer one, and is prepared again against what is actually stored.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(vocabulary): choose the words a story practises from real evidence
entry.content:
feat(vocabulary): choose the words a story practises from real evidence

Selection is pure and random only through the injected source: recency is a
membership some source established, never an age computed here. Tiers are drawn
uniformly, candidates are ordered canonically first so the read order of two
sources cannot change a seeded draw, and a short pool returns fewer targets
rather than padding a focus list with unrelated vocabulary.

entry.title: feat(vocabulary): carry what a source proved about practice into storage
entry.content:
feat(vocabulary): carry what a source proved about practice into storage

Recent-study evidence now reaches the vocabulary it describes. Each word keeps
the pools it was found in, merged across the notes that produced it, and each
source's cache keeps the capture that established them: when it was read, which
questions it could answer, and whether its day boundaries were Anki's own.

The basis lives on the capture rather than on the word because that is where the
difference belongs. A word without evidence means "not practised" for a source
that ran the searches and "never asked" for one that could not, and a single
optional flag on the word cannot hold both. The cache field is required for the
same reason: a pasted word list, a package and a bridge that failed all have to
say what they observed instead of leaving an absence to be read as a no.

Schema version 12 marks every cache written before the searches existed as
unmeasured. Backfilling it from the intervals and repetition counts those rows
already carry would be exactly the inference the searches replaced.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(anki): ask Anki which words were actually practised recently
entry.content:
feat(anki): ask Anki which words were actually practised recently

Recency was inferred: first review decayed over months, or, where no review log
existed, the card's own interval. Neither survives a premade deck the learner
reset and started again, which keeps its repetitions, its first review and a
short interval whether or not it has been opened since.

Anki answers the question itself. `rated:1`, `rated:3` and `rated:7` say which
of a mapping's cards were answered in the last one, three and seven study days,
with the learner's own rollover, and `rated:7:1` and `rated:7:2` which of those
were answered Again or Hard. The five searches are bounded per mapping, two in
flight at a time, and narrowed to the mapping's own scope so nothing outside it
can reach the vocabulary through the intersection.

They are separate reads over a live collection rather than one snapshot, so the
pools are checked for the nesting they have by definition; a capture that still
disagrees with itself after one reread is reported unavailable instead of
published as fact. What a source could not establish stays distinct from what it
established as absent, per capture rather than per word, because a bridge that
cannot run the searches must leave a stated limitation and not a vocabulary that
looks unstudied. Learning state and short intervals are correlated on the card
that was actually answered, never across siblings that disagree.

The fake endpoint read only quoted search terms, so it would have answered every
`rated:` search with the whole mapping. It now implements `rated:` and Anki's
deck wildcards, and card fixtures say how long ago they were answered rather
than carrying a date the test would have to place inside a study day.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix(anki): read the card columns AnkiDroid actually publishes
entry.content:
fix(anki): read the card columns AnkiDroid actually publishes

The bridge projected `ivl`, the name of the field inside a collection file.
AnkiDroid's public contract publishes that column as `interval`, so every build
rejected the projection and the fallback turned the mistake into a successful
import with the interval silently absent — the one signal Android recency then
rested on. The test fake was built from the same assumption, so it could only
agree; the external column names are now declared independently of us.

With the projection correct, the rest of the published card contract is
readable: card type, home deck of a card studied from a filtered deck, FSRS
difficulty and the last answer, converted once from the provider's seconds. Each
is absent independently, so one column an older build does not publish no longer
costs the others, and a supported column holding null, a malformed value and an
unsupported column stay three different things inside the provider boundary.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix(anki): keep bridge card reads working without the interval column
entry.content:
fix(anki): keep bridge card reads working without the interval column

AnkiDroid fills card rows itself and rejects an unknown projection column only
once a row is produced, so probing with an id that matches nothing proved
nothing: the enriched projection was adopted and then failed on the first real
batch, which the app reported as a source that cannot show what you reviewed.

The interval projection is now given up where the failure actually appears, on
the first batch that returns rows, and the downgrade sticks so later batches
cost no failed query. A permission failure still propagates, because the legacy
retry fails the same way.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(vocabulary): say when a snapshot predates Anki word selection
entry.content:
feat(vocabulary): say when a snapshot predates Anki word selection

A snapshot built before the scheduling signals existed carries none of them, so
both priority modes score every word the same and behave exactly as Uniform
does. That is the right degradation, but in silence it is indistinguishable from
the bug this follows: the learner picks a mode, nothing changes, and nothing
says why.

One quiet line under the select, shown only when the chosen mode has nothing to
weight. A learner on Uniform is not asking for anything the snapshot cannot
give, so they see nothing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: fix(vocabulary): make Anki word selection bias the palette it promises
entry.content:
fix(vocabulary): make Anki word selection bias the palette it promises

Recently learned scored by review count, which under modern scheduling tracks
difficulty rather than age: measured against a real collection, words learned
eleven months apart scored within four per cent of each other, so choosing the
mode did nothing. It now scores by when the learner actually first reviewed the
word, decaying by half every 120 days, and falls back to the card's interval
where no review log exists.

Difficult ordered words correctly but spanned a 1.6-fold tilt across several
hundred candidates, which is invisible, and half its evidence was absent or
stale — under FSRS the ease factor freezes at whatever SM-2 last wrote. It now
prefers FSRS's own difficulty, keeping the older lapse-and-ease estimate as a
fallback confined to a band around neutral, because that estimate cannot tell an
easy word from one it knows nothing about.

Both modes reduce their evidence to a score and share one curve onto a range
sixteen times the baseline. A word with no evidence scores the midpoint, so a
snapshot predating these signals is sampled exactly as Uniform would sample it
rather than being reordered on meaningless grounds.

Candidate weights are now computed once rather than recomputed on every draw,
which cannot change a selection because they never depended on the pool.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(anki): report the card interval from the Android bridge
entry.content:
feat(anki): report the card interval from the Android bridge

AnkiDroid exposes no review log, so the bridge cannot say when a word was first
reviewed. It can say how far out the card is scheduled, which is the fallback
the palette uses to judge how recently something was learned on Android.

The column is optional in practice: an unknown projection column makes the
content provider reject the whole query, so an older AnkiDroid would lose every
card rather than one signal. The projection is therefore resolved once, after
the supported one has already proved access, so a permission or provider failure
is still reported as itself.

Also documents `queue`, which the bridge has always emitted but the action table
never listed.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>

entry.title: feat(anki): read first-review time over AnkiConnect
entry.content:
feat(anki): read first-review time over AnkiConnect

Gives the desktop path the same evidence the package path now has, by asking
`getReviewsOfCards` for the cards in each batch that already passed eligibility.
Folding it into the existing loop means one extra request per `cardsInfo` batch
and never a request about a card that was filtered out, rather than a second
pass over the collection's whole history.

`cardsInfo` also carries `interval`, which costs no extra round trip and gives
every endpoint a fallback for judging how recently a word was learned.

An endpoint that cannot answer must not cost the learner their vocabulary, so
any failure other than cancellation turns the request off for the rest of the
run, warns once, and continues on the interval alone. The Android bridge is
never asked at all: AnkiDroid exposes no review log, so the request would be a
guaranteed refusal and a misleading warning on every refresh. The protocol
fixtures record that refusal so both sides stay honest about it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
